title: X. Both Together
paragraphs: Alyosha left his father’s house more worn out and downhearted than when he had gone in. His mind felt shattered, knocked off balance. He was afraid to gather up the broken pieces and make one picture out of all the painful, clashing things this day had brought him. What he felt came close to despair, which he had never known before. Over everything else, like a mountain, loomed the fatal question that had no answer: how would it end between his father and his brother Dmitri, with this terrible woman standing between them? Now he had seen it with his own eyes. He had been present and watched the two of them face to face. And yet only his brother Dmitri could be made unhappy, terribly, completely unhappy. Trouble was waiting for him. Other people, it seemed, were involved too, and much more deeply than Alyosha could have guessed before. There was something downright mysterious in it as well. Ivan had taken a step toward him, which Alyosha had wished for a long time. Yet now, for some reason, it frightened him. And then there were the women. Strange to say, that morning he had set out for Katerina Ivanovna’s in the deepest embarrassment. Now he felt none of that. On the contrary, he was hurrying there as though he expected her to show him what to do. Yet the message he had for her was plainly harder to deliver than before. The business of the three thousand was settled beyond recall, and Dmitri, feeling dishonored and with his last hope gone, might stoop to anything. He had also told Alyosha to describe to Katerina Ivanovna the scene that had just taken place with his father.

By now it was seven o’clock and growing dark when Alyosha reached Katerina Ivanovna’s house on the High Street, a very roomy, comfortable house. He knew that she lived there with two aunts. One of them, a woman with little education, was the aunt of her half-sister Agafya Ivanovna, and had looked after Katerina Ivanovna in her father’s house when she came home from boarding school. The other aunt was a Moscow lady of style and consequence, though badly off. People said that both of them gave in to Katerina Ivanovna in everything, and that she kept them around only as chaperons. Katerina Ivanovna herself gave in to no one but her benefactress, the general’s widow. Illness had kept the widow in Moscow, and Katerina Ivanovna had to write to her twice a week, giving a full account of everything she did.

Alyosha stepped into the hall and asked the maid who opened the door to take up his name. It was obvious that they already knew he was there. Perhaps someone had seen him from the window. At any rate, Alyosha heard a commotion, the patter of hurrying feet and the rustle of skirts. Two or three women, it seemed, had dashed out of the room.

Alyosha found it odd that his arrival should set off such a flurry. All the same, he was shown straight into the drawing room. It was a big room, elegantly and lavishly furnished, nothing like the usual provincial style. There were sofas, lounges and settees in plenty, and tables large and small. There were pictures on the walls, vases and lamps on the tables, masses of flowers, and even an aquarium in the window. It was twilight, and rather dark. Alyosha made out a silk mantle thrown down on the sofa, where people had clearly just been sitting. On the table in front of the sofa stood two half-finished cups of chocolate, some cakes, a glass saucer of blue raisins and another of sweets. Alyosha saw that he had interrupted guests, and frowned. But just then the portière was raised, and Katerina Ivanovna came in with quick, hurrying steps, holding out both hands to him, her face radiant with delight. At the same moment a servant brought in two lighted candles and put them on the table.
“Thank God! You’ve come at last, too! I’ve been praying for you all day! Sit down.”

Alyosha had been struck by Katerina Ivanovna’s beauty three weeks earlier, when Dmitri first took him to meet her, at her own particular request. They hadn’t had any real conversation on that occasion. Taking Alyosha for very shy, Katerina Ivanovna had talked to Dmitri the whole time, to spare him. Alyosha had kept quiet, but he had seen a great deal, and seen it clearly. He had been struck by the commanding manner, the proud ease and the self-assurance of this haughty girl. All of that was certain, and Alyosha felt he wasn’t exaggerating. He thought her big, glowing black eyes very fine, especially in her pale, even rather sallow, longish face. But in those eyes, and in the lines of her exquisite lips, there was something his brother might well love passionately, but which perhaps couldn’t be loved for long. He had said almost exactly that to Dmitri after the visit, when his brother begged and insisted that he not hide what he thought of his betrothed.
“You’ll be happy with her, but perhaps not peacefully happy.”
“Just so, brother. People like that never change. They don’t bow to fate. So you think I won’t love her forever.”
“No, perhaps you’ll love her forever. But perhaps you won’t always be happy with her.”

Alyosha had said all this at the time blushing, and furious with himself for giving in to his brother’s pleading and putting such “foolish” ideas into words. The moment he had spoken, his opinion had struck him as awfully foolish. He was ashamed, too, to have spoken so confidently about a woman. That made it all the more astonishing to him now, at the first sight of Katerina Ivanovna running in to meet him, to feel that he might have been entirely wrong. This time her face shone with unforced, good-natured kindness and a direct, warm-hearted honesty. The “pride and haughtiness” that had struck him so much before now showed only as a frank, generous energy and a bright, strong faith in herself. Alyosha understood at the first glance, at the first word, that the whole tragedy of her position, in her relation to the man she loved so dearly, was no secret to her. She perhaps already knew everything, absolutely everything. And yet her face was bright, and her faith in the future was so strong. Alyosha felt at once that in his thoughts he had done her a grave injustice. He was conquered and captivated on the spot. On top of all this, he noticed from her very first words that she was in great excitement, an excitement perhaps quite out of the ordinary and close to ecstasy.
“I was so eager to see you because I can learn the whole truth from you, and from nobody else.”
“I’ve come,” muttered Alyosha, confused, “I—he sent me.”

“Ah, he sent you! I knew he would. Now I know everything, everything!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, her eyes flashing. “Wait a moment, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and I’ll tell you why I’ve wanted so badly to see you. You see, I probably know far more than you do yourself, so you don’t need to tell me anything. What I want from you is this. I want to know your own last impression of him. I want you to tell me, as directly and plainly as you can, even coarsely (oh, as coarsely as you like!), what you thought of him just now, and of his position, after meeting him today. That may be better than if I talked to him myself, since he doesn’t want to come to me. Do you see what I’m asking of you? Now tell me simply, tell me every word of the message he sent you with (I knew he would send you).”
“He told me to bring you his compliments—and to say he will never come again—but to bring you his compliments.”
“His compliments? Is that what he said—his own word for it?”
“Yes.”
“He might have used the wrong word by chance? Might he not have meant a different word?”
“No. He told me to repeat that very word. He begged me two or three times not to forget it.”
Katerina Ivanovna turned hotly red.

“Help me now, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Now I truly need your help. I’ll tell you what I think, and you must just say whether I’m right or wrong. Listen! If he had sent me his compliments offhand, without insisting that you repeat those words, without any stress on them, that would be the end of everything! But if he insisted on those words, if he made a point of telling you not to forget to give them to me, then perhaps he was in a fever, beside himself. He had made up his mind, and he was scared by it. He wasn’t walking away from me with a firm step. He was leaping headlong. The stress on that phrase may have been just bravado.”
“Yes, yes!” cried Alyosha warmly. “I think you’re right.”
“And if so, he’s not altogether lost. I can still save him. Wait! Did he say anything to you about money—about three thousand roubles?”

“He did speak of it, and that’s what is crushing him more than anything. He said he had lost his honor and nothing matters now,” Alyosha answered eagerly, feeling hope rush into his heart and believing that there really might be a way out, a rescue, for his brother. “But do you know about the money?” he added, and broke off suddenly.

“I’ve known about it for a long time. I telegraphed to Moscow to inquire, and heard long ago that the money had not come. He hadn’t sent it, but I said nothing. Last week I found out that he was still short of money. All I wanted in all this was for him to know whom to turn to, and who was his true friend. No, he won’t admit that I am his truest friend. He won’t know me. He looks on me only as a woman. I’ve been tormented all week, trying to think how to keep him from being ashamed to face me because he spent that three thousand. Let him be ashamed of himself, let him be ashamed of other people knowing, but not of my knowing. He can tell God everything without shame. Why is it that he still doesn’t understand how much I’m ready to bear for his sake? Why, why doesn’t he know me? How dare he not know me, after all that has happened? I want to save him forever. Let him forget me as his betrothed. And here he fears that he’s dishonored in my eyes. Why, he wasn’t afraid to be open with you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Why do I not deserve the same?”
She said the last words in tears. Tears poured from her eyes.
“I must tell you,” Alyosha began, his voice shaking too, “what has just happened between him and my father.”

And he told her the whole scene: how Dmitri had sent him to get the money, how Dmitri had burst in and knocked his father down, and how after that Dmitri had again, specially and emphatically, begged Alyosha to carry her his compliments and his farewell. “He has gone to that woman,” Alyosha added softly.

“And you think I can’t put up with that woman? Does he think I can’t? But he won’t marry her,” she laughed suddenly, in a nervous way. “Can a Karamazov’s passion last forever? It’s passion, not love. He won’t marry her, because she won’t marry him.” Again Katerina Ivanovna laughed oddly.
“He may marry her,” said Alyosha sadly, looking down.

“He won’t marry her, I tell you. That girl is an angel. Do you know that? Do you know that?” Katerina Ivanovna burst out with extraordinary warmth. “She is one of the most fantastic of fantastic creatures. I know how bewitching she is, but I also know she is kind, firm and noble. Why are you looking at me like that, Alexey Fyodorovitch? Maybe my words surprise you, maybe you don’t believe me? Agrafena Alexandrovna, my angel!” she called suddenly to someone, peeping into the next room, “come in here. This is a friend. This is Alyosha. He knows all about our affairs. Show yourself to him.”
“All I was doing was waiting behind the curtain until you called me,” said a soft, you might even say sugary, woman’s voice.

The portière was lifted, and Grushenka herself came up to the table, smiling and beaming. A violent revulsion went through Alyosha. He fixed his eyes on her and couldn’t take them off. Here she was, that awful woman, the “beast,” as Ivan had called her half an hour earlier. And yet the creature standing before him seemed the simplest, most ordinary woman, good-natured and kind, handsome certainly, but so like other handsome ordinary women! It was true that she was very, very good-looking, with that Russian beauty which so many men love so passionately. She was fairly tall, though a little shorter than Katerina Ivanovna, who was exceptionally tall. She had a full figure and soft, almost noiseless movements, softened to a peculiar over-sweetness, like her voice. She didn’t walk as Katerina Ivanovna did, with a vigorous, bold stride, but without a sound. Her feet made absolutely no noise on the floor. She sank softly into a low chair, softly rustling her sumptuous black silk dress and delicately nestling her milk-white neck and broad shoulders in a costly cashmere shawl. She was twenty-two, and her face looked exactly that age. Her face was very white, with a pale pink tint on the cheeks. The cast of her face might be called too broad, and the lower jaw was set a little forward. Her upper lip was thin, but the lower one, slightly prominent, was at least twice as full and looked pouting. But her magnificent, abundant dark brown hair, her sable-colored eyebrows and her charming gray-blue eyes with their long lashes would have made even the most indifferent person, meeting her by chance in a crowd on the street, stop at the sight of her face and remember it long afterward. What struck Alyosha most in that face was its look of childlike good nature. Her eyes had a childlike look, a look of childish delight. She came up to the table beaming with delight, and seemed to be expecting something, with the impatient, trusting curiosity of a child. The light in her eyes gladdened the soul—Alyosha felt that. There was something else in her which he couldn’t understand, or couldn’t have defined, and which yet perhaps affected him without his knowing it. It was the softness, the voluptuousness of her bodily movements, that catlike silence. Yet it was a strong, ample body. Under the shawl you could see full, broad shoulders and a high bosom, still quite girlish. Her figure suggested the lines of the Venus of Milo, though already in somewhat exaggerated proportions. You could guess that. Connoisseurs of Russian beauty could have said with certainty that this fresh, still youthful beauty would lose its harmony by the time she was thirty, that it would “spread”; that her face would get puffy, that wrinkles would soon appear on her forehead and around her eyes, and that her complexion might turn coarse and red. In short, it was the beauty of the moment, the fleeting beauty so often found in Russian women. Alyosha, of course, wasn’t thinking of this. But though he was fascinated, he wondered, with an unpleasant feeling and something like regret, why she drawled like that and couldn’t speak naturally. She did it evidently because she felt there was a charm in the exaggerated, honeyed lilt of the syllables. It was, of course, only a bad, low-bred habit that showed poor schooling and a false idea of good manners. And yet this tone and manner of speaking seemed to Alyosha almost incredibly out of keeping with the childishly simple and happy expression of her face, the soft, babyish joy in her eyes. Katerina Ivanovna at once sat her down in an armchair facing Alyosha, and kissed her rapturously several times on her smiling lips. She seemed quite in love with her.

“This is the first time we’ve met, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said rapturously. “I wanted to know her, to see her. I wanted to go to her, but I had barely said so when she came to me herself. I knew we would settle everything together—everything. My heart told me so. People begged me not to take this step, but I foresaw it would get us out of our difficulty, and I wasn’t wrong. Grushenka has explained everything to me and told me all she intends to do. She flew here like an angel of goodness and brought us peace and joy.”
“You didn’t look down on me, sweet, excellent young lady,” Grushenka drawled in her sing-song voice, still with the same charming, delighted smile.

“Don’t you dare talk to me like that, you sorceress, you witch! Look down on you! Here, I must kiss your lower lip once more. It looks swollen already, and now it will swell more, and more, and more. Look how she laughs, Alexey Fyodorovitch! It does your heart good to see the angel.”
Alyosha flushed, and faint shivers, hardly noticeable, kept running through him.
“You think so highly of me, dear young lady, and maybe I don’t deserve your kindness at all.”

“Not worthy! She’s not worthy of it!” Katerina Ivanovna cried again with the same warmth. “You know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we’re fanciful, we’re self-willed, but in our little heart we’re the proudest of the proud. We’re noble, we’re generous, Alexey Fyodorovitch, let me tell you. We have only been unfortunate. We were too ready to give up everything for a man who was perhaps unworthy, or just fickle. There was one man—only one, an officer too. We loved him and sacrificed everything for him. That was long ago, five years ago, and he forgot us. He married. Now he is a widower. He has written that he is coming here. And, do you know, we’ve loved him, only him, all this time, and we’ve loved him all our life! He will come, and Grushenka will be happy again. For five years now she has been wretched. But who can reproach her? Who can boast of her favor? Only that bedridden old merchant, and he is more like her father, her friend, her protector. He found her then in despair and agony, abandoned by the man she loved. She was ready to drown herself, but the old merchant saved her—saved her!”
“You’re defending me so kindly, dear young lady. You’re in such a hurry about everything,” Grushenka drawled again.

“Defend you! Is it my place to defend you? Would I dare? Grushenka, angel, give me your hand. Look at that charming soft little hand, Alexey Fyodorovitch! Look at it! It has brought me happiness and lifted me up, and I’m going to kiss it, on both sides, here, here, here!”

And three times, in a kind of rapture, she kissed Grushenka’s hand, which was certainly charming, though rather fat. Grushenka held out her hand with a charming, musical, nervous little laugh. She watched the “sweet young lady” and clearly liked having her hand kissed.
“There may be a little too much rapture here,” thought Alyosha. He blushed. All the while he felt a strange unease in his heart.
“You won’t make me blush, dear young lady, by kissing my hand like this in front of Alexey Fyodorovitch.”
“Is that what you think, that I meant to make you blush?” said Katerina Ivanovna, a little surprised. “Oh, my dear, how little you understand me!”

“Yes, and maybe you misunderstand me completely too, dear young lady. Maybe I’m not as good as I seem to you. I have a bad heart. I will have my own way. I charmed poor Dmitri Fyodorovitch that day just for fun.”
“But now you’ll save him. You gave me your word. You’ll explain it all to him. You’ll break it to him that you have loved another man for a long time, and that he is now offering you his hand.”
“Oh, no! I never gave you my word to do that. You’re the one who kept talking about it. I didn’t give you my word.”
“Then I didn’t understand you quite right,” said Katerina Ivanovna slowly, turning a little pale. “You promised—”

“Oh, no, angel lady, I haven’t promised a thing,” Grushenka interrupted softly and evenly, with the same gay, simple look. “You can see right away, dear young lady, what a willful wretch I am next to you. If I want to do something, I do it. I may have made you some sort of promise a minute ago. But now I’m thinking again: I might go back to Mitya. I liked him very much once—liked him for almost a whole hour. Now maybe I’ll go and tell him to stay with me from today on. You see, I’m so changeable.”
“Just now you said—something completely different,” Katerina Ivanovna whispered faintly.
“Ah, just now! But, you know, I’m such a soft-hearted, silly creature. Just think what he’s been through on my account! What if I get home and feel sorry for him? What then?”
“I never expected—”

“Ah, young lady, how good and generous you are next to me! Maybe now you won’t want anything to do with a silly creature like me, now that you know my character. Give me your sweet little hand, angelic lady,” she said tenderly, and with something like reverence she took Katerina Ivanovna’s hand.

“Here, dear young lady, I’ll take your hand and kiss it the way you kissed mine. You kissed mine three times, but I ought to kiss yours three hundred times to be even with you. Well, never mind that. After that it will be as God wills. Maybe I’ll be your slave completely and want to do whatever you tell me, like a slave. Let it be as God wills, without any agreements or promises. What a sweet hand—what a sweet hand you have! You sweet young lady, you incredible beauty!”
She slowly raised the hands to her lips, with the odd purpose, in fact, of “being even” with her in kisses.

Katerina Ivanovna did not pull her hand away. She listened to those last words with timid hope, though Grushenka’s promise to do her bidding like a slave was put very strangely. She looked intently into Grushenka’s eyes. She still saw in them the same simple-hearted, trusting look, the same bright gaiety.
“She may be too naïve,” thought Katerina Ivanovna, with a gleam of hope.
Meanwhile Grushenka seemed delighted with the “sweet hand.” She raised it slowly to her lips. But she held it near her lips for two or three minutes, as though reconsidering something.
“Do you know, angel lady,” she suddenly drawled in an even softer, sugarier voice, “do you know, I think I won’t kiss your hand after all?” And she gave a merry little laugh.
“As you like. What’s the matter with you?” said Katerina Ivanovna, with a sudden start.
“So that you’re left remembering that you kissed my hand and I didn’t kiss yours.”
Her eyes suddenly flashed. She looked at Katerina Ivanovna with terrible intensity.
“Insolent creature!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, as if she had suddenly understood. She flushed all over and jumped to her feet.
Grushenka got up too, but without hurrying.
“So I’ll tell Mitya how you kissed my hand and I didn’t kiss yours at all. How he’ll laugh!”
“Vile slut! Go away!”
“Oh, shame on you, young lady! Oh, shame! A word like that is beneath you, dear young lady.”
“Go away! You’re a creature for sale!” screamed Katerina Ivanovna. Every feature of her utterly distorted face was working.
“For sale, indeed! You used to go to gentlemen at dusk for money once. You brought your beauty to sell. You see, I know.”
Katerina Ivanovna shrieked and would have thrown herself at her, but Alyosha held her back with all his strength.
“Not a step, not a word! Don’t speak, don’t answer her. She’ll go away—she’ll go this minute.”
At that moment Katerina Ivanovna’s two aunts ran in at her cry, and a maid with them. They all hurried to her.
“I’ll go,” said Grushenka, picking up her mantle from the sofa. “Alyosha, darling, walk me home!”
“Go away—go away, hurry!” cried Alyosha, clasping his hands imploringly.
“Dear little Alyosha, walk me home! I’ve got a pretty little story to tell you on the way. I staged this scene for your benefit, Alyosha. Walk me home, dear, you’ll be glad you did afterwards.”
Alyosha turned away, wringing his hands. Grushenka ran out of the house with a musical laugh.
Katerina Ivanovna went into hysterics. She sobbed and shook with convulsions. Everyone fussed around her.

“I warned you,” said the elder of her aunts. “I tried to keep you from doing this. You’re too impulsive. How could you do such a thing? You don’t know women like that, and they say she’s worse than any of them. You’re too headstrong.”
“She’s a tigress!” yelled Katerina Ivanovna. “Why did you hold me, Alexey Fyodorovitch? I would have beaten her—beaten her!”
She couldn’t control herself in front of Alyosha. Perhaps, in fact, she didn’t care to.
“She should be flogged in public, on a scaffold!”
Alyosha backed toward the door.

“But, my God!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, clasping her hands. “He! He! How could he be so dishonorable, so inhuman! Why, he told that creature what happened on that fatal, accursed day! ‘You brought your beauty to sell, dear young lady.’ She knows! Your brother is a scoundrel, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”
Alyosha wanted to say something, but he couldn’t find the words. His heart was aching.
“Go away, Alexey Fyodorovitch! It’s shameful, it’s awful for me! Tomorrow—I beg you on my knees—come tomorrow. Don’t condemn me. Forgive me. I don’t know what I’ll do with myself now!”
Alyosha walked out into the street, reeling. He could have wept as she did. Suddenly the maid caught up with him.
“The young lady forgot to give you this letter from Madame Hohlakov. It’s been with us since dinnertime.”
Alyosha took the little pink envelope mechanically and, almost without realizing it, put it in his pocket.
